**Dataset lineage records where data came from and how it became the training and evaluation examples.** Reproducibility needs more than the final table: it needs source versions, transformations, selection rules, labels, and split assignments. [1](https://research.google/pubs/the-ml-test-score-a-rubric-for-ml-production-readiness-and-technical-debt-reduction/)[2](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml)

Suppose a churn model uses customer features measured on a prediction date. A warehouse query run today may contain corrected records and later events that were unavailable on that date. Re-running the same SQL text is not enough to reproduce the original training set or establish that its features were available at prediction time.

Record immutable source snapshots or version identifiers, transformation code revisions, schema, filters, random seeds, join rules, and time cutoffs. For time-dependent features, distinguish event time from the time the system learned about the event. Point-in-time joins should honor the information available at the intended prediction moment.

Preserve row or group assignments to training, validation, and test splits. Recomputing a random split after adding rows can move old examples into a different partition, invalidating comparisons. For entities such as users or devices, a grouped split may be necessary to avoid leakage between related observations. [5](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html)

A content hash can verify that bytes match, but it does not explain whether the data is meaningful or lawful to use. Pair hashes with human-readable semantics: units, label definition, missing-value interpretation, and expected population. A column remaining `float` does not detect a change from dollars to cents.

**A useful replay test:** start from the recorded versions in a clean environment and reconstruct the feature table and evaluation result within a declared tolerance. Exact training weights may still vary with nondeterministic computation, so separate data reproducibility from numerical reproducibility. Link the resulting dataset identity to the registered model version and release bundle. That lets an observed production error be traced back to the inputs and decisions that produced the model. [3](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/randomness.html)[4](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/ml/model-registry/)
